newsitem.title: BRAZIL: INTERVIEW - Brazil awaits open window for new bond.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Brazil awaits open window for new bond.

text.p: Brazil has no immediate financial need to return to global debt markets, but it might consider launching another large bond should the right conditions emerge, Central Bank director Gustavo Franco said.

"We have to look at what happens in the next months to see if there is another window for us to go abroad for another sizeable issue. If there is no window, no problem, we don't issue," Franco told Reuters in an interview.

Each of Brazil's last three large sovereign-debt issues, including a $750 million global bond in October, have come at a time when international reserves were declining slightly because of capital outflows.
That condition, Franco explained, allowed the government to issue debt and bring in dollars to the economy without setting the stage for accelerated inflation.
With almost $60 billion in reserves, Brazil has no pressing financial need to issue new debt, said Franco, the Central Bank's international affairs director.

Nevertheless, large sovereign bonds are worth issuing because they allow Brazil to present its economic picture to investors, set benchmarks and "challenge our credit rating, which we think is worse than it should be," he said.
Brazil's October global bond, rated a below-investment-grade B-plus by Standard & Poor's Corp, has traded on par with or at narrower spreads than higher-rated Mexican and Argentine paper.
Brazilian officials have said that is an sign that the market has a more favorable view of Brazil risk than rating companies such as S&P's and Moody's Investors Service Inc.

Although Franco stressed that Brazil would not issue a large bond unless the government faced a period of sustained capital outflows and declining reserves, he said the country would not be a stranger to global debt markets.
Brazil would continue to place small amounts of debt in various markets and currencies to smooth the way for Brazilian banks, corporations and state-owned companies to borrow, he said.
"We will continue to do like we did last year, with small issues in pounds sterling and escudos just to open up new markets," Franco said.
